title: Instagram Trials 90-Minute Horizontal Videos, Boosting Podcasters and Creators' Reach
body:
Instagram is rolling out a limited test of a new 90‑minute horizontal video format, giving a select group of U.S. creators the chance to publish long‑form content that mimics the feel of traditional video podcasts. The move signals the social‑media giant’s ambition to become a more viable home for extended‑duration programming, positioning itself against platforms such as YouTube, Spotify and Apple Podcasts that already dominate the long‑form audio‑visual market.

The trial, which began this Monday, allows participating creators to upload videos up to an hour and a half in length, displayed in a landscape orientation that aligns with the typical viewing experience on televisions and computer monitors. By shifting away from Instagram’s signature vertical feed, the company hopes to attract audiences who prefer a cinematic layout for deeper storytelling, interviews, and discussion‑based content. Early adopters include a mix of podcasters, lifestyle influencers, and niche entertainers who have previously relied on other services to host their longer episodes.

Industry analysts view the experiment as part of a broader strategy to keep users within the Instagram ecosystem for more of their media consumption. Over the past two years, the platform has expanded its video capabilities—from 15‑second Stories to Reels, and now to IGTV, which was later folded back into the main feed. Each iteration has aimed to capture a slice of the burgeoning short‑form and long‑form video markets. With the rise of “podcast‑style” video content on TikTok and the growing appetite for on‑the‑go listening, Instagram’s horizontal format could bridge the gap between quick social snippets and the more immersive experience of a traditional podcast.

The test also raises questions about monetization and creator incentives. Instagram currently offers limited direct revenue tools for video creators beyond brand partnerships and the occasional ad placement in Reels. If the horizontal video feature proves popular, the platform may need to develop a more robust ad‑sharing model or integrate subscription‑based options to compete with the revenue streams available on rival services. Moreover, the algorithmic feed that powers Instagram’s discovery engine will need to be recalibrated to surface longer content without overwhelming users accustomed to rapid scrolling.

From a user perspective, the shift could reshape how audiences discover and engage with podcasts. Historically, listeners have turned to dedicated audio platforms or YouTube for visual podcasts, often navigating separate apps to find the content they want. By embedding longer videos directly into Instagram’s familiar interface, the company could streamline the consumption journey, encouraging casual viewers to dip into longer formats without leaving the app. However, the success of this approach will hinge on the platform’s ability to balance discoverability with the risk of cluttering users’ feeds with lengthier material that may not align with their browsing habits.

Looking ahead, Instagram’s experiment may set the stage for a more integrated entertainment hub that blends social interaction, short‑form reels, and full‑length video podcasts under one roof. If creators and audiences respond positively, the network could expand the horizontal video capability beyond the United States, eventually making it a permanent fixture. Such a development would reinforce Instagram’s evolution from a photo‑sharing service to a comprehensive media destination, challenging established players and reshaping the competitive landscape of digital content distribution.
